Chapter 3: Grabbing Attention with the Unexpected
So, once you’ve got an idea that’s clear and simple, there’s still one big hurdle—how do you actually get someone to notice? In today’s world, we’re all constantly bombarded with messages. It’s exhausting, right? That’s why the unexpected is so powerful. Surprises have a way of cutting right through all that noise, breaking through the mental filters we use to protect ourselves from information overload.
Here’s how it works. Unexpectedness grabs us by violating our expectations. When something doesn’t fit the usual pattern, it creates a moment that makes us stop and pay attention. It’s almost like our brains say, “Wait, what just happened?” That jolt out of autopilot is where true attention begins. But there’s a trick—it can’t just be surprise for its own sake. If it distracts from your main point, it’s not doing you any favors. The surprise has to reinforce the core message, not overshadow it.
Think about safety campaigns. You’ve probably heard the phrase, “Speed kills,” so many times it barely registers. But what if, instead, you saw a dramatic image—a crumpled car with an empty child’s seat in the back? That kind of unexpected visual forces you to confront the real consequences. The surprise draws you in, and the message sticks with you long after.
So, how can you use the unexpected to your advantage? Well, here are a few ideas:
First, break a pattern. Start with something that challenges what people expect, maybe even turns an assumption on its head.
Next, create curiosity. Ask a question or introduce a mystery that people just have to resolve.
And finally, deliver a twist. Share information in a way that surprises, but also makes your main point even clearer.
Now, curiosity is like the cousin of surprise. When we notice a gap in what we know, we’re driven to fill it. That’s why mysteries and puzzles are so irresistible—they build up a little tension that can only be relieved by learning more. When you frame your message as a question or a challenge, you’re inviting people to lean in and stay engaged.
Imagine a science teacher starting class by asking, “Why do astronauts float in space?” That question instantly creates a knowledge gap. The students want the answer, and when they finally hear it, it sticks—because it solved a puzzle they cared about.
So, here’s the real takeaway: use surprise and curiosity as tools, not just tricks. When the unexpected is woven into the heart of your idea, it doesn’t just grab attention. It makes your message unforgettable.
